# Language structure {#sec-m1-linguagem} This chapter covers the minimum of the language needed for the rest of the course. The idea is not to cover R exhaustively, but to recognise the objects we work with and know how to inspect them. ## Objects and assignment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tku <- 1250.75 # assignment uf <- "PR" tku #> [1] 1250.75 class(tku) #> [1] "numeric" class(uf) #> [1] "character" ``` ::: Everything in R is an object, and every object has a **class**. When something goes wrong, the first question is always `class()`. Most of the time, the problem is that a number is stored as text. ## Vectors The vector is the basic structure: a sequence of values **of the same type**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ufs <- c("AM", "PR", "SP", "BA") tkus <- c(4213386.6, 8332538649.4, 1600854068.7, 1560549752.2) length(ufs) #> [1] 4 tkus[2] # indexing starts at 1 #> [1] 8332538649 tkus[c(1, 3)] #> [1] 4213387 1600854069 tkus[tkus > 2e9] # logical indexing: base R's filter #> [1] 8332538649 ufs[tkus > 2e9] #> [1] "PR" ``` ::: The types you meet day to day (the names on the left are in Portuguese: numeric, integer, text, logical, date, factor): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} c( numerico = class(1.5), inteiro = class(1L), texto = class("PR"), logico = class(TRUE), data = class(as.Date("2026-09-28")), fator = class(factor("Conteinerizada")) ) #> numerico inteiro texto logico data fator #> "numeric" "integer" "character" "logical" "Date" "factor" ``` ::: **Silent coercion** is the main source of errors in real data: if a single value is text, the whole vector becomes text. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(1, 2, "3") class(x) #> [1] "character" x * 2 # error: the vector became text #> Error in `x * 2`: #> ! non-numeric argument to binary operator as.numeric(x) * 2 # explicit fix #> [1] 2 4 6 ``` ::: And the missing value, `NA`, propagates: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(10, NA, 30) mean(y) #> [1] NA mean(y, na.rm = TRUE) #> [1] 20 is.na(y) #> [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE sum(is.na(y)) #> [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} `NA` is "I don't know the value"; `NULL` is "does not exist"; `NaN` is the invalid result of a calculation (`0/0`); and `Inf` is infinity (`1/0`). `is.na()` is the check you will use almost always. ::: ## Factors A factor is text with a fixed and **ordered** set of categories. It matters because the order of the levels sets the order of the bars in a chart and of the columns in a table. The categories below are the ANTAQ cargo profiles: container, dry bulk and liquid bulk. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} perfil <- factor( c("Granel Sólido", "Conteinerizada", "Granel Líquido", "Conteinerizada"), levels = c("Conteinerizada", "Granel Sólido", "Granel Líquido") ) levels(perfil) #> [1] "Conteinerizada" "Granel Sólido" "Granel Líquido" table(perfil) #> perfil #> Conteinerizada Granel Sólido Granel Líquido #> 2 1 1 as.integer(perfil) # the internal code of each level #> [1] 2 1 3 1 ``` ::: ## Matrices A matrix is a vector with two dimensions. It is the natural structure for an **origin–destination matrix**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} od <- matrix( c( 0, 120, 340, 95, 0, 210, 310, 180, 0), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(origem = c("AM", "PR", "SP"), destino = c("AM", "PR", "SP")) ) od #> destino #> origem AM PR SP #> AM 0 120 340 #> PR 95 0 210 #> SP 310 180 0 dim(od) #> [1] 3 3 od["AM", "SP"] # flow AM -> SP #> [1] 340 rowSums(od) # total produced by origin #> AM PR SP #> 460 305 490 colSums(od) # total attracted by destination #> AM PR SP #> 405 300 550 t(od) # transpose #> origem #> destino AM PR SP #> AM 0 95 310 #> PR 120 0 180 #> SP 340 210 0 ``` ::: In module 3 we will swap `matrix` for **sparse** matrices (`Matrix::sparseMatrix`), which store only the pairs with flow. That is essential when there are thousands of zones. ## Lists A list holds elements of different types, including other lists. It is what most models and routing functions return. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cenario <- list( nome = "Cabotagem 2025", ano = 2025L, ufs = c("AM", "PR", "SP"), matriz = od ) names(cenario) #> [1] "nome" "ano" "ufs" "matriz" cenario$ufs #> [1] "AM" "PR" "SP" cenario[["matriz"]]["PR", "SP"] #> [1] 210 str(cenario, max.level = 1) #> List of 4 #> $ nome : chr "Cabotagem 2025" #> $ ano : int 2025 #> $ ufs : chr [1:3] "AM" "PR" "SP" #> $ matriz: num [1:3, 1:3] 0 95 310 120 0 180 340 210 0 #> ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2 ``` ::: ## `data.frame` This is the table: a list of columns of the same length. Practically the whole course revolves around it. From here on, the examples use a real extract of ANTAQ's coastal shipping dataset that reappears in the rest of the module, instead of made-up numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx") fluxos <- data.frame( origem = bruto[["UF de Origem"]], destino = bruto[["UF de Destino"]], tku = bruto[["TKU\n(t x km)"]] ) # a real extract: one row from each of these origin states, plus one # small shipment, so that the three TKU bands appear in the example alvo <- c("AM", "PR", "SP", "BA", "SC", "RS") pequeno <- which(fluxos$tku >= 5e5 & fluxos$tku < 1e6)[1] fluxos <- fluxos[c(match(alvo, fluxos$origem), pequeno), ] rownames(fluxos) <- NULL fluxos ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} dim(fluxos) #> [1] 7 3 names(fluxos) #> [1] "origem" "destino" "tku" str(fluxos) #> 'data.frame': 7 obs. of 3 variables: #> $ origem : chr "AM" "PR" "SP" "BA" ... #> $ destino: chr "PR" "PE" "AM" "AM" ... #> $ tku : num 4.21e+06 3.59e+08 5.08e+09 9.34e+08 1.26e+09 ... ``` ::: Quick inspection of any table: the four commands you **always** run when you open a new dataset: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(fluxos, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fluxos) #> origem destino tku #> Length :7 Length :7 Min. :7.255e+05 #> N.unique :6 N.unique :4 1st Qu.:1.818e+08 #> N.blank :0 N.blank :0 Median :9.336e+08 #> Min.nchar:2 Min.nchar:2 Mean :1.352e+09 #> Max.nchar:2 Max.nchar:2 3rd Qu.:1.542e+09 #> Max. :5.078e+09 nrow(fluxos); ncol(fluxos) #> [1] 7 #> [1] 3 sapply(fluxos, class) #> origem destino tku #> "character" "character" "numeric" ``` ::: Accessing columns and rows in base R: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos$tku #> [1] 4213386.6 359411740.4 5078241178.2 933586360.9 1258614769.2 #> [6] 1826132222.5 725465.9 fluxos[["tku"]] #> [1] 4213386.6 359411740.4 5078241178.2 933586360.9 1258614769.2 #> [6] 1826132222.5 725465.9 fluxos[1, ] # first row ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos[, c("origem", "tku")] # two columns ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos[fluxos$tku > 2e9, ] # filter ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Operators and comparisons ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 2 + 3; 10 / 4; 2^10; 7 %% 3; 7 %/% 3 #> [1] 5 #> [1] 2.5 #> [1] 1024 #> [1] 1 #> [1] 2 3 == 3; 3 != 4; 3 < 4 #> [1] TRUE #> [1] TRUE #> [1] TRUE TRUE & FALSE; TRUE | FALSE; !TRUE #> [1] FALSE #> [1] TRUE #> [1] FALSE "PR" %in% c("PR", "SC", "RS") # belongs to #> [1] TRUE ``` ::: `%in%` is base R's most useful operator for working with data: it selects everything that is in a list of codes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sul <- c("PR", "SC", "RS") fluxos[fluxos$destino %in% sul, ] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Conditionals The function below classifies a TKU value as high (`"alto"`), medium (`"médio"`) or low (`"baixo"`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} classificar <- function(tku) { if (is.na(tku)) { "sem informação" } else if (tku >= 1e9) { "alto" } else if (tku >= 1e6) { "médio" } else { "baixo" } } classificar(fluxos$tku[3]) # SP -> AM, the largest shipment in the extract #> [1] "alto" classificar(fluxos$tku[7]) # the small shipment we set aside #> [1] "baixo" ``` ::: `if` works with **one** value. For vectors, use `ifelse()` or `dplyr::case_when()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ifelse(fluxos$tku >= 1e9, "alto", "não alto") #> [1] "não alto" "não alto" "alto" "não alto" "alto" "alto" "não alto" dplyr::case_when( fluxos$tku >= 1e9 ~ "alto", fluxos$tku >= 1e6 ~ "médio", .default = "baixo" ) #> [1] "médio" "médio" "alto" "médio" "alto" "alto" "baixo" ``` ::: ## Functions Writing functions is what saves you from copying and pasting the same snippet five times. And that is where errors pile up when you don't. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #' Converts TKU to billions of TKU #' @param tku numeric vector in t x km #' @param digitos decimal places tku_bi <- function(tku, digitos = 2) { if (!is.numeric(tku)) stop("`tku` precisa ser numérico.") round(tku / 1e9, digitos) } tku_bi(fluxos$tku) #> [1] 0.00 0.36 5.08 0.93 1.26 1.83 0.00 tku_bi(fluxos$tku, digitos = 3) #> [1] 0.004 0.359 5.078 0.934 1.259 1.826 0.001 ``` ::: Things to notice: arguments with a **default value** (`digitos = 2`), input **validation** (`stop()`) and the fact that the function returns the value of the last expression. ## Iteration ### `for` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} for (uf in c("AM", "PR", "SP")) { total <- sum(fluxos$tku[fluxos$origem == uf]) cat(uf, ":", tku_bi(total), "bi TKU\n") } #> AM : 0 bi TKU #> PR : 0.36 bi TKU #> SP : 5.08 bi TKU ``` ::: ### The `apply` family ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sapply(fluxos[, "tku", drop = FALSE], mean) # returns a vector #> tku #> 1351560732 lapply(c(1e6, 1e9), function(x) sum(fluxos$tku > x)) # returns a list #> [[1]] #> [1] 6 #> #> [[2]] #> [1] 3 vapply(fluxos[, "tku", drop = FALSE], mean, numeric(1)) # with a guaranteed type #> tku #> 1351560732 ``` ::: A very common pattern in practice: **read several files and stack them**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arquivos <- list.files("dados/brutos", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) lista <- lapply(arquivos, readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) base <- dplyr::bind_rows(lista, .id = "arquivo") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Vectorise before iterating In R, vectorised operations are faster and more readable than loops. Instead of going through rows to add two columns, write `df$a + df$b`. Keep `for` for tasks that depend on a previous step (running a model per scenario, saving files, calling an API). ::: ## The `|>` *pipe* The *pipe* passes the result on the left as the first argument of the function on the right. It turns nested code into a sequence of steps readable from top to bottom. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # without pipe round(mean(fluxos$tku, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e9, 2) #> [1] 1.35 # with pipe fluxos$tku |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) |> tku_bi() #> [1] 1.35 ``` ::: You will also find `magrittr`'s *pipe*, `%>%`, in older material. For what we will do, the two are equivalent; we will use the native one, `|>`, which needs no package. ## Scripts and algorithms A script is the recipe: the steps, in order, with comments that say **why** each one exists. The structure we recommend for any Ministry analysis: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 01-leitura.R # Goal: read ANTAQ's coastal shipping dataset and standardise columns # Author: Last updated: 2026-09-28 # Input: dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx # Output: dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 1. packages ---- library(dplyr) library(readxl) # 2. reading ---- bruto <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx") # 3. standardisation ---- base <- bruto |> janitor::clean_names() # 4. checks ---- stopifnot(nrow(base) > 0, !any(is.na(base$tku_t_x_km))) # name produced by clean_names() # 5. writing ---- saveRDS(base, "dados/cabotagem_limpa.rds") ``` ::: `stopifnot()` in the middle of the script is a practice worth the effort: if an assumption stops holding when the dataset is updated, the script stops where the error is instead of silently producing a wrong number.
